title: Look at What Has Grown
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer uses autumn as a prompt for the seventh step of her Leadership Connection Model, Reflect and Refocus. She observes that people tend to save reflection for December, January or a birthday, whereas nature simply begins revealing what has grown. She invites readers to take stock of what they sowed, what took root and what never caught, and to ask whether they are enjoying the fruits of their labor. The essay then widens the lens from personal growth to impact on others: choices, habits and organizational decisions become part of the environment other people live within, often in ways the decision-maker cannot see. She is careful to say this does not mean being responsible for everything, only that we are more connected than we remember. She sets up October as a month to explore that theme and closes with reflection questions and an invitation to notice one's harvest before deciding what to plant next.
points: Reflection does not need to wait for a calendar marker; any season can serve as a prompt to take stock of what has actually grown.
The harvest questions (what took root, what flourished, what never caught) offer a simple honest inventory that includes disappointments as well as pride.
Leadership extends beyond self-development: our habits, tolerances and decisions shape the conditions other people must live and work within.
Consequences of a seemingly personal choice may ripple into someone else's workload, belonging or opportunity, even though the leader is not responsible for everything.
Her practical invitation is to notice and be honest about the harvest first, and only then decide what to plant next.
quotes: Yet we have a funny habit of assigning reflection to particular places on the calendar. We wait for December. Or January. Or a birthday.
Nature does not seem to work that way. Autumn arrives and simply begins revealing what has grown.
In the Leadership Connection Model, Step Seven is Reflect & Refocus. It is the point at which we look at what has happened, notice what we have learned, and decide what we want to create next.
What we grow does not only affect us. Our choices create experiences for other people. Our habits shape families and workplaces.
A choice that feels entirely personal to me may ripple into someone else’s day, opportunity, workload, sense of belonging, or ability to flourish.
This does not mean we are responsible for everything. It means we are connected to far more than we sometimes remember.
You do not need to decide yet what you will plant next spring. First, look at what has grown.
